title: When are you intermediate and what it means programming wise (for bodybuilding)
summary: Defines an intermediate in bodybuilding not by strength numbers but by knowledge (compounds, variations, some isolation) and mindset: the moment you start tinkering with your own program toward a clear physique goal. Intermediates should raise volume and frequency, tailor exercises to their goals, train within a 70-90% intensity window, and start managing diet, sleep, alcohol and stress. He claims most lifters quit at the novice-to-intermediate transition, blaming rushed powerlifting novice programs, and argues bodybuilders should stay novices longer.

claims.claim: For bodybuilding, an intermediate has intimate knowledge of full-body compound movements, experience with their variations, and at least some contact with isolation exercises.

In powerlifting you can become an intermediate doing only bench, squat and deadlift, which makes sense when tested on three arbitrary lifts, but physique-focused lifters shouldn't follow the powerlifting mindset.
He used to do powerlifting but no longer does.
Novices should get comfortable with a few compounds that suit their body and leverages, use variations to add volume without repeating the same stance, and do isolation.
Becoming an intermediate means having enough hypertrophy to see where your body is heading and to choose a direction; dictating precisely how your body develops is for advanced bodybuilders.
What he enjoys about bodybuilding is the freedom: no mandatory lifts or standards, as long as it fits your goals.
Being intermediate isn't tied to how much you lift or your muscle size; it's a mindset that starts the day you decide to modify your program to better fit your goals.
His novice program exists to launch people into self-programming.
Intermediates should be comfortable with volume training: at the end of a workout the total tonnage should show it was genuinely rough.
Stay within an intensity window that is neither too easy (junk volume) nor so heavy that form breaks down: usually 70-90% of 1RM, though he dislikes percentages.
To program as an intermediate, take your novice program and raise volume and frequency, add variations of lifts you like, and change isolation work, all tailored to your physique goal.
If your goal is massive arms, your program should have lots of curls and skull crushers, just as a powerlifter with a weak bench should bench at high frequency.
Average novices don't need to care much about diet beyond watching protein; intermediates must manage calories (less to look drier, more to be fuller) so the kitchen doesn't undo their training.
Intermediates must control alcohol, sleep hours and stress, which all damage gains.
Novices benefit from being kept in a 'box' where someone thinks for them; an intermediate breaks out of the box by choice to experiment and find what works.
He still discovers what works for him and drops things he's done for years.
By his own admittedly made-up estimate, about 95% of people quit lifting during the move from novice to intermediate.
He blames popular powerlifting novice programs that rush progression so hard that lifters quit when they plateau.

Many intermediates get demoralised because they can't progress; if you make it to intermediate, you'll probably stay in lifting for good, and the intermediate phase lasts much longer than the novice phase unless you're a genetic freak.
As a novice everything works with your eyes closed; as an intermediate you start consuming information from everywhere and become aware of your own evolution.

Bodybuilders should stay novices much longer than powerlifters, spend less time as intermediates and then be 'advanced forever', because they focus on volume earlier; a longer novice phase reduces the odds of quitting at the intermediate stage.
